name: Mortise and tenon wood joint construction

steps.title: Measure workpiece dimensions accurately (measure twice)
steps.visual_criteria: Steel rule or tape measure used to measure workpiece lengths; dimensions checked twice against design drawing

steps.title: Mark shoulder cut lines and tenon layout
steps.visual_criteria: Try square and marking knife used to scribe crisp, perpendicular reference lines around all four faces

steps.title: Tenon shoulder and cheek handsaw cut
steps.visual_criteria: Workpiece clamped firmly in bench vise; tenon saw cuts along waste side of line with clean perpendicular kerf

steps.title: Chisel mortise cavity and clean cheeks
steps.visual_criteria: Mortise chisel held vertical, bevel inward; mortise cavity chopped to uniform depth with flat floor and clean walls

steps.title: Dry fit and apply wood glue assembly
steps.visual_criteria: Joint test-fitted square (90 degrees); wood glue applied evenly to tenon cheeks and mortise walls, clamped tight

scenario_questions.text: Why must you always cut on the waste side of the marked reference line when sawing a tenon?
expected_points: Accounts for the width of the saw kerf (blade thickness)
Prevents the tenon from becoming loose or undersized

scenario_questions.text: What hand safety rule must you always observe when using sharp bench chisels?
expected_points: Keep both hands behind the cutting edge at all times
Clamp the workpiece securely to the bench instead of holding it with one hand

scenario_questions.text: How do you verify that a mortise and tenon joint is square before the adhesive sets?
expected_points: Use an engineer or try square on internal corners

common_mistakes: Cutting on the line instead of the waste side resulting in loose fit
Chiseling toward oneself or holding workpiece by hand in front of chisel
Uneven mortise depth preventing full shoulder seating
Applying adhesive before dry-fitting the assembly
